title: extcap: Read stdout and stderr during capture
description:
extcap: Close capture session after extcap finishes 

Wait up to 30 seconds for extcap process to finish after closing pipes.
The wait is achieved in non-blocking fashion, i.e. the UI is completely
responsive during the wait. Only actions related to capture process like
capture control, file open, save, export are inactive during the wait.

On Windows extcap child watch callback gets called immediately as the
process is forcefully terminated. Prior to this change the extcap was
forcefully terminated on Windows anyway.

The wait is possible on UNIX systems if extcap does handle SIGPIPE and
SIGTERM signals. The defaults handlers for SIGPIPE and SIGTERM simply
terminate the process so for large number of extcaps there is no change.
If extcap does not finish within 30 seconds, it is forcefully terminated
using SIGKILL signal.

wsutil: Use GIOChannel for standard pipes

Remove ws_read_string_from_pipe() as this function encourages bad design
and is no longer necessary. Extcap stderr is read only after the child
process has finished and thus the read will never block.

Close process information thread handle right away as we don't use it.
Remove unused ws_pipe_t member variables.

extcap: Read stdout and stderr during capture

Read extcap stdout/stderr data when available to prevent extcap hang on
stdout/stderr write. Discard stdout data as it was not used earlier.
Store up to 1024 bytes of stderr and display it to user after capture
stops.

Fixes #17827

Would it make sense to decrease the timeout? 30 seconds is a subjectively long time to wait for an unresponsive UI.

Can you describe how to shut down properly in docbook/wsdg_src/WSDG_chapter_capture.adoc?

It is proposal, I was not able to make better estimation. The issue is that wireshark nor extcap knows how long graceful shutdown can last.

E.g. ciscodump must discard commands and responses from Cisco device and then must remove configuration it entered before. On slow link it can last more than 20 seconds. On the other hand, when extcap terminates sooner, everything finishes immediately. So 30 seconds is just last chance. But yes, unresponsive UI :-(

I consider the UI to be fairly responsive while waiting for timeout. However because it is not graceful shutdown anyway (the pipe is closed before extcap can notice that capture is stopping), I will change the SIGKILL timeout to 3 seconds on Linux and call `TerminateProcess()` immediately on Windows.

Thinking a bit more about it, the 30 seconds in current implementation is reasonable on Linux, but not on Windows.

It is not reasonable on Windows, because the extcap might not notice the pipe being closed and thus it will take full 30 seconds. Some extcaps that actively write to pipe but don't care about broken pipe (e.g. randpktdump with sufficently low packet delay) will also take 30 seconds. For that reason, keeping the status quo on Windows (close pipes and `TerminateProcess()` right away) seems ok-ish for 4.0 release.

It is reasonable on Linux, because extcap does receive `SIGTERM` signal (and `SIGPIPE`) and the default signal handler exits the process. Therefore, the 30 seconds timeout will happen if and only if the extcap in question installed both `SIGTERM` and `SIGPIPE` handlers and for whatever reason takes long time after handling the signals. We have to have some deadline and 30 seconds sounds fair enough to me. My gut feeling is that majority of extcaps will terminate shortly (due to lack of custom `SIGTERM` and/or `SIGPIPE` handlers) and extcaps that take their time have a valid reason to do so.

Regarding the UI responsiveness, the wait is implemented with GLib mainloop event. The control does return to the mainloop before the timeout hits and thus other events work. The user can navigate the packet list just fine. Only selected actions (capture control, file open, save, export, statistics capture file properties, quit) are not possible before the extcap finishes.

@geraldcombs Is it fine to leave it at 30 seconds given the above explanation?

I wouldn't consider this as a graceful shutdown. It is basically a cleanup for the (now obsolete) workaround for missing child watch callback. The workaround is no longer needed since !7499 and !7558.

> @geraldcombs Is it fine to leave it at 30 seconds given the above explanation?

Sure. Disabling capture and file operations for up to 30 seconds isn't ideal, but it's much better than locking up the entire UI.

@desowin I am working on a console window for extcap, which would reside underneath Tools, similar to Lua->Console. So far it works great and I can get to the stderr messages, but for whatever reason stdout does not seem to trigger properly. How did you test that part of the code? Just so I know if I did something wrong there.

And for testing I just amended extcap_example.py so that the last few lines of pcap_fake_package would look like that:

```
    pcap += message

    print("Sending message", file = sys.stderr)
    print("Printing message", file = sys.stdout)

    return pcap
```

I am getting the "Sending message", both in my interface and after the capture has finished, but I am not seeing "Printing message", which means it must not have been transmitted properly? Not sure - it was a while since I last daddled with extcap python/parser stuff - but could it be, that it does not send at all? Also, seeing nothing in the terminal btw

I just added printf in `randpkt_loop()` and both stdout and stderr work fine. Note that the stdout data is simply discarded after extcap process finishes. The data is discarded because there was no use for it and as the extcap has already finished, the extcap won't get stuck outputting stdout.

To retrieve buffered data after extcap finishes, add `extcap_stdout_cb()` loop inside `extcap_child_watch_cb()` before `g_io_channel_unref(pipedata->stdout_io);`.

Note that multiple extcaps can be capturing simultaneously, so the invoke callback should have the information from which extcap the data comes from.

My change is during runtime, it does not save up over time. It simply does not register for stdout on macOS, so it seems capturing stdout does not work. I tried your approach for randpkt and the same thing happened (or rather did not). 

The data would not get discarded, as it is saved and stored in the UI during capture, therefore it has nothing to do anymore at that point with the extcap subsystem. It simply never got captured by extcap in the first place, suggesting your change not having the right effect on macOS. 

I never want to retrieve the data after the extcap finished, as this would void the whole point of the console being a debugging tool. It should always capture while it is still running. Which is the reason for using extcap_example, because that tool runs until you stop it.

To distinguish between multiple ext caps, I am adding the interface name to the message, as that is a unique identifier

I am able to reproduce the issue with Python on Linux. The problem is that python never outputs the data. The solution is to force flush.
```
    print("Sending message", file = sys.stderr, flush = True)
    print("Printing message", file = sys.stdout, flush = True)
```
That was it, thanks!
Presumably in most instances above where the word "Linux" is used, "UN\*X" is meant - i.e., the test is "not Windows", not "Linux".
